central_reading: The filter account (Trika kañcuka ontology) treats agency-limitation (kalā-kañcuka) and knowledge-limitation (vidyā-kañcuka) as categorically distinct metaphysical dimensions — kalā contracts universal agency into limited efficacy, vidyā contracts universal knowledge into limited cognition. Predictive Processing treats both agency (precision of action-outcome predictions) and knowledge (precision of perceptual priors) as variations in a single graded precision-weighting parameter. This difference is testable: if kalā and vidyā are categorically distinct, independent factorial manipulation of agency and knowledge should produce dissociable behavioural signatures (agency selective effects on intentional binding, knowledge selective effects on metacognitive efficiency) that cannot be reduced to a single latent precision dimension. The proposed Agency-Knowledge Dissociation Task (AKDT) operationalises this as a 2×2 within-subjects factorial design with agency (75% vs 25% action-outcome contingency) and knowledge (80% vs 55% cue validity) as factors, using meta-d' as the shared behavioural readout, with Bayesian model comparison (single-parameter vs two-parameter models) as the decisive test.

nyaya_reading.hetu: The six kañcukas (kalā, vidyā, rāga, niyati, kāla, māyā) are described in Tantrāloka as orthogonal limitation dimensions each constraining a distinct aspect of universal consciousness. If they were merely parametric variations of a single restriction mechanism, their distinctions would dissolve under factorial experimental manipulation that independently modulates agency and knowledge.
nyaya_reading.sadhya: Independent factorial manipulation of agency and knowledge will produce dissociable behavioural signatures — agency effects on intentional binding and sense-of-causality without corresponding shifts in metacognitive efficiency, knowledge effects on metacognitive efficiency without corresponding sense-of-causality shifts — that cannot be captured by a single latent precision parameter within standard PP models.

nyaya_reading.hetu: Standard PP models treat both agency (sense of control) and knowledge (perceptual certainty) as expressions of precision weighting on prediction error — the same computational parameter with different contextual applications. If they are categorically distinct dimensions (as per kañcuka ontology), independently manipulating each while holding the other constant should produce dissociable effects beyond what a single precision parameter can capture, and this is testable with existing behavioural paradigms (intentional binding for agency, cue validity for perceptual precision) within a single factorial design.
nyaya_reading.sadhya: The AKDT can distinguish categorical from graded accounts with N ≥ 64 participants, α = 0.05, 1−β = 0.80 for the interaction term (anticipated f = 0.25), using meta-d′ as the shared behavioural readout and ΔLOO-IC decision thresholds for Bayesian model comparison (single-parameter PP model vs two-parameter categorical model), with pre-registered stopping rules for each outcome.

nnexpr_mappings.falsifier: The agency manipulation (75% vs 25% contingency) fails to produce a measurable shift in intentional binding magnitude under the specified parameters, rendering the agency factor ineffective and the factorial design degenerate. Or: the best-fitting Bayesian model across all participants is the single-parameter model (ΔLOO-IC < 2 relative to the two-parameter alternative), and the ANOVA interaction term is non-significant (η² < 0.06, p > 0.05). Or: meta-d′ proves insensitive to the knowledge manipulation under the 80/55% cue validity contrast, requiring a different readout that breaks the shared-measurement-space requirement.

If the factorial experiment yields a significant interaction or dissociable main-effect patterns beyond what a single precision parameter can capture, the PP graded-precision account of the agency/knowledge boundary is falsified at the phenomenological-behavioural level, requiring additional categorical structure not predicted by standard active inference models.
